[0] Privacy search engine company DuckDuckGo has released a new survey highlighting how much personal information users share with AI chatbots, and how many people have only a vague understanding of how these conversations are handled. Below are the survey details.

[1] Survey shows AI users share more data than they realise

[2] In a survey published today, DuckDuckGo revealed multiple privacy concerns about users' use of AI chatbots, including that nearly one in three users have told an AI something they would not say to a friend, family member, colleague, or healthcare professional. Among those who identified as AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

[3] Here is what DuckDuckGo had to say:

[4] The company noted that among a sample of nearly 2,000 U.S. adult respondents, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots default to using conversations to train models, while only 25% knew that law enforcement could obtain AI conversation records via a court subpoena.

[5] The findings also reveal a striking behavioural gap between parents and non-parents: parents or guardians with children at home confide in AI at almost double the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo said that "among parents who use AI, 43% have told an AI something they have never shared with anyone else," while "among AI users without kids at home, this figure drops to 25%."

[6] DuckDuckGo argues that AI companies, through advertising and media appearances, encourage users to treat chatbots as confidants, but these conversations may not be as private as users have been led to believe.

[7] On the question of trust, the survey found that major AI companies only barely outranked the U.S. government when it came to confidence in protecting user data. However, suspicion of both was high: 39% of respondents said they had no confidence at all in large AI companies, while 48% had no confidence at all in the government.

[8] Finally, DuckDuckGo noted that users still have an opportunity to change how they approach AI privacy, especially as chatbot usage habits remain relatively new:

[9] When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people think, "It's too late, my data has already been exposed." But the most valuable piece of information you can share with big tech is your next question, not the one you asked yesterday, last month, or years ago. So it is never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services.

[10] The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer, more transparent data-handling policies.
